opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, fundraising has been one of the most surprising parts of becoming a founder for me. I came from a math background, where you sit with a problem for months and the only thing that matters is whether your proof is correct. Fundraising is almost the opposite. You have maybe thirty minutes, sometimes less, to convey a vision that you've been thinking about for years, and the other person is making a judgment about you as much as about the idea.

At first I treated it a bit like a qualifying exam. I prepared very thoroughly and anticipated every technical question. Then I realized investors usually aren't trying to verify a theorem. They're trying to understand: Why this problem? Why now? Why you? And can this team actually build something that matters? So I learned to tell the story more clearly. For us, the story is that mathematics is a uniquely good testbed for reasoning, because you can formally verify whether something is right. That makes it a place where AI can genuinely self-improve, and that matters far beyond math.

Emotionally, it's a roller coaster. You have days with several great conversations, and then days where people don't get it at all. I try not to take either too personally. A "no" often says more about someone's thesis or timing than about whether your idea is good. And a "yes" isn't the finish line. It's the start of a relationship where you now owe people progress.

The thing I value most is that fundraising forces clarity. Every time I pitch, I find a sharper way to explain what we're doing, and sometimes a hard question from an investor changes how I think about the roadmap. So I've come to see it less as asking for money and more as finding partners who believe in the same future. When it works, it feels like recruiting, just for a different kind of teammate.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, fundraising for me has been less about pitching and more about finding people who already see the same thing you see. When I started Axiom, I wasn't going in trying to convince investors that AI for math was a good idea. I was looking for the people who, when I described what we wanted to do, would lean forward instead of politely nodding.

I think a lot of founders treat it like an exam, like you have to get the right answer for each investor. I came from a math background, so my instinct at first was to over-prepare, to have a proof for every objection. But the conversations that actually worked were the ones where I was just being very direct about what I believed and where the uncertainty was. Good investors can tell when you're performing confidence versus when you actually have conviction and have thought about what could go wrong.

The other thing I'd say is it's emotionally strange. You'll have one meeting where someone tells you this is the most important problem they've ever heard, and the next meeting someone tells you it's impossible or that no one will pay for it, and both happen the same afternoon. You have to hold your own view steady through that. For me the anchor was always going back to the technical reality: what have we actually built, what do the results actually show. If that's solid, the noise matters less.

And I'll admit, as a young founder and as a woman in a very technical field, there were moments where I felt I had to establish credibility before I could even get to the substance. That gets tiring. But over time I realized the best thing I could do was just talk about the math and the research with the same depth I'd use with a colleague. The people worth working with respond to that. The ones who don't, you probably didn't want on your cap table anyway.

astra-6.text:
For me, fundraising is a process of learning how to communicate what I see. As a founder, you spend so much time thinking about a problem that you can forget how much context someone else needs. You have to explain why this matters, why now, and why you’re the right person to build it.

It can also feel very personal. You care deeply about what you’re building, so it takes practice to hear a no without treating it as a verdict on you or the company. I think the useful thing is to stay open to feedback while keeping your own judgment. Sometimes a question exposes something you haven’t thought through; sometimes it just tells you that you and that investor see the opportunity differently.

And you’re evaluating them, too. You’re looking for someone you can have an honest conversation with when things aren’t going well, because that’s when the relationship really matters.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, fundraising is a process of learning how to communicate what I’m building. You might have a very detailed picture in your head, but you have to make it clear to someone who’s encountering it for the first time: Why does this matter? Why now? And why are you the person to do it?

It can also feel quite personal. You care deeply about the company, so it takes practice to hear a no without treating it as a judgment of you. I try to stay curious about the feedback while remembering that not every investor will be the right fit. Ultimately, you’re looking for someone you can work with through uncertainty, beyond the fundraising itself.
